lesson.menu_title: Third Conditional -- The Decision You Would Make Differently
lesson.menu_desc: Answer the hardest question in a senior interview with the past that never happened -- if we had..., we would have... -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- Third Conditional for the Decision Review
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Lucia Nishiyama Serra | Lesson 13 -- Third Conditional for the Decision Review

listenings.text: Before we start, one ground rule. This is a retrospective, not a trial. Nobody in this room is going to be blamed for a decision that looked reasonable in March. Here is my own reading of it. We chose the bigger rollout because the vendor promised a six-week timeline, and we believed that promise without checking it. That was the assumption, and nobody tested it. If we had run a smaller test first, we would have found the gap in week two, and the fallout would have been a short delay instead of a lost quarter. Second thing. Priya flagged the cost risk on the fourteenth of February. I read the email and I moved on, because we were all watching the schedule. Cost was our blind spot. If I had taken that email seriously, we would have course-corrected three months earlier. So, two changes going forward. Every rollout starts with a small test, and every flagged risk gets a written answer within a week. Now I want to hear your reading of it.

There is one interview question that senior candidates handle badly, and it is always the same one. Tell me about a decision you would make differently. Half the candidates get defensive and say there is nothing they would change, which tells the interviewer that they do not learn. The other half apologize for four minutes, which is worse. Here is the shape that works, and it is only three sentences. One. Name the decision and the assumption behind it, in the past simple. Two. Say what would have happened if you had chosen differently, and that sentence is a third conditional. If we had run a smaller test, we would have caught the problem in week two. Three. Say what you changed because of it, in the present. Now, one word of grammar, because this is exactly where Brazilian candidates lose points. The word would never goes inside the if half of the sentence. If we would have flagged it is not English. It is if we had flagged it, and then would have on the other side. Get that one right and you sound like someone who has thought about the mistake, instead of someone still living inside it.

extra_audio.text: In March we chose the full rollout, because the vendor promised a six-week timeline. Nobody tested that assumption, and one engineer flagged the cost risk in February. We underestimated the migration, and the fallout lasted two quarters. If we had run a smaller test, we would have caught the problem in week two. Today every rollout starts with a test, and every flagged risk gets a written answer.
